The Amazing Echo

At one o'clock, Priya was finally allowed to put on her costume. She pulled on some grey leggings and a grey long-sleeved top. For her hands there were grey mittens with little felt claws sewn onto the fingertips.

She looked at her homemade mask and the row of cardboard spikes glued along the hood and hoped they looked at least a little bit like an echidna. The last thing she had to put on was a cape which her father had sewn out of an old brown bedsheet. On the back was a huge letter 'E' painted in bright orange.

When she was ready, she curled herself into a tight ball and rolled across the lounge room floor before her mum scooped her up and stood her on the ottoman.

'Look! Down on the ground! Is it a soccer ball? Is it a hedgehog?'

Priya's father answered, 'No, it's the Amazing Echo!'

Priya jumped down from the ottoman and pulled off her mask. She was feeling a bit grumpy. 'I'd still rather have a real echidna than pretend to be one,' she muttered.

Her parents looked at each other. Her mum patted the spare cushion on the couch and said, 'Come and sit down, Echo. We've got some good news for you.' She nudged her husband. 'You tell her, Raj.'

As Priya sat down, her father put his arm around her and said, 'When you get home from the party, there'll be a surprise waiting for you. Mum's going out soon and she'll bring it back with her.'

Priya immediately began bouncing on the cushion, yelling, 'No way, no way! I can't wait!' Then she stopped long enough to ask, 'What is it? Is it a pet? An echidna? It is, isn't it?'

But her mum only winked at her and said, 'You'll just have to wait and see, munchkin. By the way, bring the birthday boy's present with you - I think he'll want to see your costume too.'

Priya jumped up. 'Can I go over and tell Oscar now? He asked me to get there early.'

'Well, it won't take you long to walk next door,' said her dad. 'But I think you're forgetting something.'

'What?'

'The present.'

'Whoops, sorry.' She picked up a parcel from the coffee table and hugged her dad. He straightened her cardboard spikes.

'Now don't forget to say thank you to Oscar's mother, and be careful not to trip on your cape,' he said.

'Have a good time, Echo,' said her mum, 'and don't curl up into a ball in the middle of the party.'

How to build a castle

In 1997, a man named Michel Guyot decided he wanted to find out exactly how medieval castles were built - so he set out to build one himself, entirely from scratch. He chose an abandoned quarry site in the Guedelon forest, in the Burgundy region of France, as the location for his thirteenth-century-style castle.

A team of around fifty people began the enormous task of bringing the castle to life. It wasn't simply a matter of drawing up plans and hiring workers, though: Guyot wanted the build to be as historically authentic as possible, so he insisted that only tools and techniques available in the Middle Ages could be used. He estimated the whole project would take around twenty-five years, meaning the castle wouldn't be finished until sometime in the 2020s.

Decades later, work is still underway. Visitors walking through the site today see workers shaping stone and timber entirely by hand, using no electric tools at all. Following medieval methods, the builders construct simple wooden pulleys* to hoist heavy stone blocks up to the level they're working on. Blacksmiths hand-forge the chisels used to shape timber beams, and labourers form human chains to carry baskets of earth up handmade staircases to build up the floor of the Great Hall. Inside, the stone walls are rendered** with lime to create a weatherproof seal, then smoothed with plaster, and finally decorated first with detailed line drawings and then with colourful murals painted using natural dyes. Elsewhere, the floors are being laid with kiln-fired tiles, while carpenters and blacksmiths work on the castle's doors.

Beyond the castle walls and the workers' huts lies a recreated thirteenth-century farm, where sheep wander freely, chickens scatter noisily, and pigs wallow in the mud, seemingly unbothered by the crowds of curious visitors who come to watch. Cattle and horses are kept secure inside handmade wooden fences.

Walking around the site really does feel like stepping back into the Middle Ages. Which, of course, is exactly the point.

* wheels used with ropes or chains to lift or lower heavy objects

After all the scheming we'd done to get this far, I was fairly confident nobody would guess which path we'd taken.

'We can't stop here,' said Priya, her voice low but firm. 'We're too close, and it's too open. We'll rest properly once we reach the fence line, okay? Get our heads straight.'

We looked at each other and nodded in silent agreement.

We walked three abreast now, side by side, with steady, careful steps. Nobody spoke. I, for one, was glad of the quiet. I was still trying to process what we'd just pulled off.

I glanced left, then right. Priya's serious expression cracked for just a second as she flashed me a quick, reassuring grin. Her face was streaked with dust, but she looked completely unshaken. Noah marched on without a word, his scuffed sneakers thudding steadily, giving nothing away. Braver than I'd realised, now that I thought about it. Both of them were.

Island restoration

Ever since rats began travelling the world alongside human sailors, they have caused enormous damage to the natural world. Rats don't just spread disease and raid human food stores - they also prey on smaller native animals, particularly on islands where local wildlife often has no natural defences against them.

Islands are especially vulnerable to this kind of damage. Because of their isolation, a very high proportion of island species are endemic, meaning they are found nowhere else on Earth. Although islands make up only around 5% of the planet's total land area, they are home to roughly 20% of all mammal, reptile and bird species. Tragically, about 75% of all animal extinctions recorded since the year 1600 have happened on islands, and introduced rats are usually the main culprit.

In recent decades, a growing conservation movement has worked to remove rats and other introduced predators from islands entirely, giving native wildlife a genuine chance to recover. This process is known as island restoration, and the basic idea is simple: eliminate the introduced predators, then reintroduce native species if they haven't already disappeared. New Zealand leads the world in this work, having successfully cleared rats from more than 40 islands since the 1960s. Today, roughly 800 islands worldwide are considered rodent-free, and on most of them, native animal populations have bounced back strongly.

One of the largest and most expensive island restoration projects ever attempted took place on remote South Georgia Island, near Antarctica, where an international team used a ship, three helicopters and around 100 tonnes of rat bait to eliminate the island's rat population. The project was approved because rats had already wiped out roughly 90% of the island's seabirds, and melting glaciers - retreating faster than expected - were opening up access to the last remaining safe breeding colonies.

Despite its successes, island restoration isn't without its critics. Some animal-rights advocates argue it's wrong to kill one group of animals to fix a problem that humans caused in the first place. Others point to the enormous cost involved: transporting equipment to remote islands is expensive, many islands have inaccessible terrain where rodents can hide, and specially trained detector dogs are often required to confirm a project's success. There are also concerns about the unintended effects of large-scale poisoning - in some past projects, native rodents and even land crabs were accidentally poisoned, and on the Aleutian Islands, birds of prey were poisoned after eating already-poisoned rats.

However you view it, island restoration involves deliberately killing some animals to save others. But when the alternative may be permanent extinction for many island species that exist nowhere else on Earth, is it really the wrong choice to make?

She'd dropped every single book onto the footpath and shoved him hard enough that he'd stumbled backwards into a hedge. She'd arrived home with a grass stain on her sleeve and her hair sticking up on one side.

Her younger twin brothers, Milo and Theo, who always got home from school half an hour before her, were unimpressed. 'Let us handle the fighting when it's actually necessary,' they told her solemnly.
